records.source: Ἢ ἀγνοεῖτε, ἀδελφοί, γινώσκουσιν γὰρ νόμον λαλῶ, ὅτι ὁ νόμος κυριεύει τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐφ’ ὅσον χρόνον ζῇ;
records.gloss: Or are you ignorant, brothers, to those knowing for law I speak, that the law rules over the man for as long time [as] he lives?
pieces: Surely you understand, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, since I am speaking to people who know the law, that the law is master over someone only while that person is alive.

L.1: Or do you not know, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} (for I am speaking to those who know [the] law), that the law rules over a person for as long as [that person] lives?

R.1: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, you know about the law. So you know that the law has power over people only while they are alive.

decisions.choice: Or: a new question that carries on from 6:14
alternatives: a fresh start with no link to chapter 6
decisions.reason: "Or" ties the chapter to what came before. In 6:14 Paul said that believers are "not under law but under grace"; now he shows from the law itself why its rule over them has ended.

decisions.choice: those who know the law: the law of Moses
alternatives: law in general, including Roman law
decisions.reason: Paul's readers in Rome, Jewish and Gentile believers alike, knew the Scriptures read in the synagogues, and the rest of the chapter is about the law of Moses (7:7). The word has no article, so some take it as law in general, a principle true of any legal system, Roman law included. The point is the same either way: law binds only the living.

decisions.choice: rules over: is master over
decisions.reason: kyrieuō is to be lord over someone. Paul used it in 6:9 (death no longer rules over Christ) and 6:14 (sin will not rule over you); now it is the law's rule that ends.

decisions.choice: the person lives, not the law
alternatives: as long as the law lives (is in force)
decisions.reason: The subject of "lives" is the person the law rules over. Grammatically it could be the law, but the illustration in verses 2-3 is about a person who dies.

decisions.choice: Surely you understand (B); you know (R)
decisions.reason: The question expects the answer "yes, we know", so Balanced and Readable say it as a statement. Literal keeps the question and the opening "Or".

records.heading: Free from the law

records.source: ἡ γὰρ ὕπανδρος γυνὴ τῷ ζῶντι ἀνδρὶ δέδεται νόμῳ· ἐὰν δὲ ἀποθάνῃ ὁ ἀνήρ, κατήργηται ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου τοῦ ἀνδρός.
records.gloss: The for married woman to the living husband has been bound by law; if but should die the husband, she has been released from the law of the husband.
pieces: Take a married woman: the law binds her to her husband while he is alive. But if he dies, she is set free from the law that tied her to him.

L.2: For the married woman is bound by law to the living husband; but if the husband dies, she is released from the law of the husband.

R.2: For example, the law says that a married woman must stay with her husband while he is alive. But if her husband dies, that law no longer holds her.

decisions.choice: a married woman bound to her husband by the law
decisions.reason: hypandros means "under a husband", that is, married. Under the law of Moses a wife was bound to her husband, and it was the husband who could end the marriage (Deuteronomy 24:1-4); only his death set her free without question.

decisions.choice: released: the law no longer has any claim on her
decisions.reason: katargeō means to make ineffective or to release. The perfect tense says she stays released. Paul uses the same verb of believers in verse 6: "we have been released from the law".

decisions.choice: the law of the husband: the law that binds her to her husband
decisions.reason: The genitive means the law as it concerns the husband, the marriage law, not a law that the husband made.

decisions.choice: Take a married woman (B); For example (R)
decisions.reason: "For" introduces an illustration of verse 1. Balanced and Readable say so.

records.source: ἄρα οὖν ζῶντος τοῦ ἀνδρὸς μοιχαλὶς χρηματίσει ἐὰν γένηται ἀνδρὶ ἑτέρῳ· ἐὰν δὲ ἀποθάνῃ ὁ ἀνήρ, ἐλευθέρα ἐστὶν ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου, τοῦ μὴ εἶναι αὐτὴν μοιχαλίδα γενομένην ἀνδρὶ ἑτέρῳ.
records.gloss: So then, being alive the husband, an adulteress she will be called if she becomes to another man; if but should die the husband, free she is from the law, so that not to be her an adulteress having become to another man.
pieces: So if she joins herself to another man while her husband is still living, people will call her an adulteress. But once her husband has died she is free from the law, and marrying another man does not make her an adulteress.

L.3: So then, while the husband is alive, she will be called an adulteress if she becomes another man's; but if the husband dies, she is free from the law, so that she is not an adulteress if she becomes another man's.

R.3: So if she marries another man while her husband is still alive, she is guilty of adultery. But if her husband dies, she is free from that law. Then she can marry another man, and it is not adultery.

decisions.choice: become another man's: marry or live as his wife
decisions.reason: "To become to a man" is a Greek way, taken from the Greek Old Testament, of saying a woman is joined to a man as his wife (Deuteronomy 24:2). Paul uses the same words of believers in verse 4: they now belong to another.

decisions.choice: she will be called: she will bear the name publicly
decisions.reason: chrēmatizō here means to be known by a name. The point is how the law and the community would judge her.

decisions.choice: so that she is not an adulteress: the result of her freedom
decisions.reason: The infinitive clause gives the result of being free from the law: a second marriage after her husband's death is not adultery.

decisions.choice: joins herself to / marrying (B); marries (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say plainly what "becomes another man's" means (m1). Literal keeps the Greek expression so that the link with verse 4 can be seen.

records.source: Ὥστε, ἀδελφοί μου, καὶ ὑμεῖς ἐθανατώθητε τῷ νόμῳ διὰ τοῦ σώματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ, εἰς τὸ γενέσθαι ὑμᾶς ἑτέρῳ, τῷ ἐκ νεκρῶν ἐγερθέντι ἵνα καρποφορήσωμεν τῷ θεῷ.
records.gloss: So, brothers of me, also you were put to death to the law through the body of the Christ, for the to become you to another, to the [one] from dead [ones] having been raised, so that we may bear fruit to God.
pieces: It is the same with you, my {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}. Through the body of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} you were put to death as far as the law is concerned, so that you could be joined to another: to the one who was raised from the dead. And so we can bear fruit for God.

L.4: So then, my {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, you also were put to death to the law through the body of the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, for you to become another's, [belonging] to the one raised from [the] dead, so that we might bear fruit for God.

R.4: My {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, it is the same with you. When {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} died on the cross, you died with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and the law lost its hold on you. Now you belong to someone else, to the one who was raised from death. So now our lives can produce good things for God.

decisions.choice: So then: the point of the illustration
decisions.reason: Paul applies verses 2-3. The picture does not match at every point (there the husband dies, here believers die), but the point holds: a death ends the law's claim and leaves a person free to belong to another.

decisions.choice: through the body of Christ: through his death on the cross, which believers share
alternatives: through belonging to the church, Christ's body
decisions.reason: Believers died with Christ when he died in his body (6:3-8; Colossians 1:22). Some see a reference to the church as Christ's body, but the setting is death and resurrection.

decisions.choice: belonging to another: the marriage picture applied to Christ
decisions.reason: "To become another's" repeats the words used of the woman's second marriage in verse 3. Believers now belong to the risen Christ, as a wife to her husband (compare 2 Corinthians 11:2).

decisions.choice: bear fruit: a life that pleases God
alternatives: bear children, continuing the marriage picture
decisions.reason: The image is of fruit, the outcome of a life (6:21-22). Some hear the marriage picture continued, with offspring born to the new union, but Paul does not develop that thought.

decisions.choice: you ... we: Paul includes himself
decisions.reason: Paul turns from "you" to "we" at the end, joining himself to his readers, as he does again in verses 5-6.

decisions.choice: put to death as far as the law is concerned
decisions.reason: "Put to death to the law" means that the law no longer has any claim on them. Balanced spells out the dative so that it does not sound as if the law did the killing.

decisions.choice: When the Messiah died on the cross, you died with him ... produce good things for God
decisions.reason: Readable explains "through the body of Christ" (m2) and the fruit image (m4) with words from 6:3-8.

records.source: ὅτε γὰρ ἦμεν ἐν τῇ σαρκί, τὰ παθήματα τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν τὰ διὰ τοῦ νόμου ἐνηργεῖτο ἐν τοῖς μέλεσιν ἡμῶν εἰς τὸ καρποφορῆσαι τῷ θανάτῳ·
records.gloss: When for we were in the flesh, the passions of the sins, the [ones] through the law, were at work in the members of us for the to bear fruit to the death;
pieces: When we lived in the flesh, the law stirred up sinful desires in us. They were at work in the parts of our bodies, and what we produced belonged to death.

L.5: For when we were in the flesh, the passions of sins, which [came] through the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death;

R.5: Before, when our sinful selves were in control, the law only stirred up our desire to sin. Those desires were at work in our bodies, and what they produced led to death.

decisions.choice: in the flesh: the old life, human life under sin's sway
decisions.reason: Here "flesh" is not the body but human life in its weakness, ruled by sin and set against the Spirit. Paul speaks of it as past: in 8:9 he says believers "are not in the flesh but in the Spirit".

decisions.choice: passions of sins: passions that lead to sins
decisions.reason: The genitive describes the passions by what they produce: desires that issue in sinful deeds.

decisions.choice: through the law: the law provoked them
decisions.reason: The law did not create these passions, but its commands gave sin a way to stir them up. Paul explains how in verses 7-11, and insists that the law itself is not sin.

decisions.choice: members: the parts of the body
decisions.reason: As in 6:13 and 6:19, the members are the parts of the body through which a person acts.

decisions.choice: bear fruit for death: produce what ends in death
decisions.reason: This is the opposite of verse 4. The old life produced a harvest that belonged to death, as 6:21 says: "the end of those things is death".

decisions.choice: when our sinful selves were in control
alternatives: in the flesh
decisions.reason: Readable says what "in the flesh" means here (m1), with "sinful self" as in Romans 13:14 and Galatians 5. Literal and Balanced keep "flesh".

decisions.choice: the law stirred up sinful desires
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make the law the subject of a verb to say what "passions ... through the law" means (m3). Literal brackets the verb it supplies.

records.source: νυνὶ δὲ κατηργήθημεν ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου, ἀποθανόντες ἐν ᾧ κατειχόμεθα, ὥστε δουλεύειν ἡμᾶς ἐν καινότητι πνεύματος καὶ οὐ παλαιότητι γράμματος.
records.gloss: Now but we were released from the law, having died [to that] in which we were held, so as to serve us in newness of spirit and not oldness of letter.
pieces: But now we are free from the law. We have died to what once held us fast, so that we serve in the new life of the Spirit, not in the old life of the written letter.

L.6: But now we have been released from the law, having died to that by which we were held, so that we serve in newness of [the] Spirit and not in oldness of [the] letter.

R.6: But now we are free from the law. We died, and what held us prisoner has no more power over us. So now we serve God with the new life the Spirit gives, and not in the old way of obeying written rules.

decisions.choice: that by which we were held: the law
alternatives: sin, or the old life in the flesh
decisions.reason: "Having died to that in which we were held" most naturally refers to the law just named: believers have died to it (verse 4). Some take it as sin or the old life, which also held them captive (6:6, 7:5).

decisions.choice: serve: serve as slaves serve a master
decisions.reason: douleuō is the verb of slavery. Believers still serve, but as slaves of God (6:22), in a new way.

decisions.choice: Spirit: God's Spirit
alternatives: the human spirit, inward life
decisions.reason: Spirit and letter are set side by side as in 2:29 and 2 Corinthians 3:6, where the Spirit is God's Spirit. The word could mean the human spirit, but chapter 8 takes up the Spirit's work at length.

decisions.choice: letter: the written law
decisions.reason: gramma is what is written: the law as a code of written commands, with no power to give life (2 Corinthians 3:6). It does not mean the "literal sense" of a text.

decisions.choice: released: the law has no more claim
decisions.reason: The same verb as in verse 2, where the widow is released from the law of her husband.

decisions.choice: the new life of the Spirit ... the old life of the written letter
alternatives: newness of the Spirit ... oldness of the letter
decisions.reason: Balanced turns the abstract nouns "newness" and "oldness" into the life each one describes.

decisions.choice: serve God ... obeying written rules
decisions.reason: Readable names the one served (God, as in 6:22 and 7:25) and explains "letter" (m4).

records.source: Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν;
records.gloss: What then shall we say?
pieces: What then are we to say?

R.7: So what should we say about this?

decisions.choice: a question that leads to an objection
decisions.reason: Paul uses this question to raise an objection his teaching could provoke (as in 6:1 and 9:14). Verse 5 said the passions came "through the law"; does that make the law itself evil?

records.heading: The law and sin

records.source: ὁ νόμος ἁμαρτία;
records.gloss: The law sin?
pieces: Is the law sin?

R.7: Does this mean the law is sinful?

decisions.choice: Is the law itself sin?
decisions.reason: The objection is that if the law stirs up sinful passions (verse 5) and increases trespass (5:20), the law must be sinful. Paul rejects this at once.

records.source: μὴ γένοιτο· ἀλλὰ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν οὐκ ἔγνων εἰ μὴ διὰ νόμου, τήν τε γὰρ ἐπιθυμίαν οὐκ ᾔδειν εἰ μὴ ὁ νόμος ἔλεγεν· Οὐκ ἐπιθυμήσεις·
records.gloss: May it not be; but the sin not I knew except through law; the then for desire not I had known except the law was saying: Not you shall covet.
pieces: Certainly not! But it was the law that taught me what sin is. I would never have recognized wrong desire for what it is unless the law had said, "You shall not covet."

L.7: May it not be! Rather, I did not know sin except through [the] law; for I would not have known desire if the law had not said, "You shall not covet."

R.7: Of course not! But without the law, I would not have known what sin is. I would not have known that wanting what belongs to others is wrong if the law had not said, "Do not long for what is not yours."

decisions.choice: "I" in 7:7-25: a speaker whose identity is debated; the text keeps "I"
alternatives: Paul's own experience
Adam
Israel under the law
any person under the law
decisions.reason: From here to the end of the chapter Paul speaks as "I". Who this "I" is has long been debated. He may be telling his own story as a Jew who met the law's command; or speaking as Adam, who received the first command, was deceived and died (verses 9-11 echo Genesis 2-3); or as Israel, which received the law at Sinai; or as anyone who lives under the law without the Spirit, a figure of speech in which a writer says "I" to draw the reader in. In verses 14-25 a further question arises (see 7:14). The text is translated with "I" at every level, so that readers can weigh the question themselves.

decisions.choice: Exodus 20:17 and Deuteronomy 5:21
decisions.reason: Paul quotes the tenth commandment from the Greek Old Testament, but only its first words, without the list of a neighbor's house, wife and goods. Shortened like this, it forbids wrong desire as such.

decisions.choice: desire: craving for what God has forbidden
decisions.reason: epithymia and the verb in the commandment share a root. The word can mean any strong desire; here it is the desire the commandment forbids, the root of other sins.

decisions.choice: I did not know ... I would not have known: knowing sin as sin
decisions.reason: The first verb says that the law is how the speaker came to know sin; the second, with the condition that follows, says what would have been true without the law. Knowing here is recognition: the law shows sin for what it is (3:20).

decisions.choice: Certainly not! (B); Of course not! (R)
decisions.reason: The same rendering as in 3:4, 3:31 and 9:14. Literal keeps "May it not be!"

decisions.choice: wanting what belongs to others ... Do not long for what is not yours
decisions.reason: "Covet" is not an everyday word, so Readable says what it means.

records.source: ἀφορμὴν δὲ λαβοῦσα ἡ ἁμαρτία διὰ τῆς ἐντολῆς κατειργάσατο ἐν ἐμοὶ πᾶσαν ἐπιθυμίαν, χωρὶς γὰρ νόμου ἁμαρτία νεκρά.
records.gloss: An opening but having taken the sin through the commandment produced in me every desire; apart from for law sin [is] dead.
pieces: Sin found its opening in the commandment and used it to rouse every kind of wrong desire in me, for without the law sin is dead.

L.8: But sin, having found an opening through the commandment, worked in me every desire; for apart from [the] law sin [is] dead.

R.8: But sin used the command as a chance to attack. Through the command, sin made me want all kinds of wrong things. Without the law, sin has no power.

decisions.choice: opening: a starting point for an attack
decisions.reason: aphormē was used of a base from which an army sets out. Sin is pictured as an enemy that finds in the commandment a place to launch its attack.

decisions.choice: through the commandment goes with what sin did
alternatives: sin found an opening through the commandment
decisions.reason: "Through the commandment" can go with "finding an opening" or with "produced". Verse 11 has the same order and adds "through it" to the verb, so the sense is the same either way: the commandment was the tool sin used.

decisions.choice: sin: a power that acts
decisions.reason: As in chapters 5-6, sin is spoken of as a power with a will of its own, which deceives and kills (verse 11). The law is its tool, not its source.

decisions.choice: dead: inactive, without power
decisions.reason: Sin is not absent without the law, but it lies idle, unable to show itself as rebellion against a command (compare 4:15, 5:13).

decisions.choice: a chance to attack ... has no power
decisions.reason: Readable explains the military picture (m1) and what "dead" means here (m4).

records.source: ἐγὼ δὲ ἔζων χωρὶς νόμου ποτέ· ἐλθούσης δὲ τῆς ἐντολῆς ἡ ἁμαρτία ἀνέζησεν, ἐγὼ δὲ ἀπέθανον, καὶ εὑρέθη μοι ἡ ἐντολὴ ἡ εἰς ζωὴν αὕτη εἰς θάνατον·
records.gloss: I but was living apart from law once; having come but the commandment, the sin came to life again, \v 10 I but died, and was found to me the commandment, the [one] for life, this [one] for death;
pieces: There was a time when I lived without the law. Then the commandment arrived, sin woke up and came alive,
and I died. The commandment was given for life, yet for me it led to death.

L.9: And I was once alive apart from [the] law; but when the commandment came, sin came back to life,
L.10: and I died; and the commandment that [was] for life, this very [one] was found to be for death to me;

R.9: At one time I lived without the law. Then the command came. Sin woke up,
R.10: and I died. God gave the command to bring life, but it brought me death.

decisions.choice: alive ... died: a change in standing before God, not bodily death
alternatives: Adam in the garden
Israel before Sinai
Paul as a child, before he was bound to keep the law
decisions.reason: Being alive apart from the law and then dying describe what happened when the command came. Read as Adam, the words recall life in the garden before the command was broken; read as Paul or Israel, they describe life before the law's demand was known, and the death that sin brought (see the note on the speaker at 7:7).

decisions.choice: came to life: sprang into action
decisions.reason: anazaō can mean to come back to life, which would fit Adam and the earlier sin of the world. Many take it more simply as "came alive": sin, dead until then (verse 8), woke up.

decisions.choice: the commandment for life: Leviticus 18:5
decisions.reason: The law promised life to those who keep it: "the person who does them will live by them" (Leviticus 18:5, quoted in 10:5). In Genesis 2:17 the command too was tied to life and death.

decisions.choice: was found to be: turned out to be
decisions.reason: The passive verb says what the commandment proved to be in the speaker's experience, not what it was meant to be.

decisions.choice: was given for life (B); God gave the command to bring life (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say whose purpose the words "for life" express. The giver is God (verse 22 "the law of God").

records.source: ἡ γὰρ ἁμαρτία ἀφορμὴν λαβοῦσα διὰ τῆς ἐντολῆς ἐξηπάτησέν με καὶ δι’ αὐτῆς ἀπέκτεινεν.
records.gloss: The for sin, an opening having taken through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed [me].
pieces: Sin found its opening in the commandment, deceived me, and used the commandment to kill me.

L.11: For sin, having found an opening through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed [me].

R.11: Sin used the command to trick me, and then it used the command to kill me.

decisions.choice: deceived: an echo of Genesis 3:13
decisions.reason: In Genesis 3:13 Eve says, "The serpent deceived me", and Paul uses this same verb of Eve in 2 Corinthians 11:3. Here sin plays the serpent's part, using God's command to bring death. The echo supports, but does not prove, the reading of the "I" as Adam (see 7:7).

decisions.choice: sin, not the law, is the killer
decisions.reason: Verse 8 is repeated with stronger verbs: sin deceived and killed. The law was the tool; sin was the one who used it.

decisions.choice: killed [me]
decisions.reason: The Greek leaves the object of "killed" to be understood from "deceived me".

records.source: ὥστε ὁ μὲν νόμος ἅγιος, καὶ ἡ ἐντολὴ ἁγία καὶ δικαία καὶ ἀγαθή.
records.gloss: So the indeed law [is] holy, and the commandment holy and righteous and good.
pieces: The law, then, is holy. The commandment is holy, just and good.

L.12: So the law [is] holy, and the commandment [is] holy and righteous and good.

R.12: So the law is holy. Its command is holy and fair and good.

decisions.choice: indeed: the first half of a contrast
decisions.reason: The particle men looks for a "but" that never comes in this sentence. The other side follows in verse 13: the law is good, but sin used it.

decisions.choice: the commandment: the command just quoted, standing for the law
decisions.reason: Paul has spoken of one command, "You shall not covet". What is true of it is true of all God's commands.

decisions.choice: righteous: just, right in what it requires
decisions.reason: dikaios here describes the commandment: what it asks is fair and right.

decisions.choice: just (B); fair (R)
alternatives: righteous
decisions.reason: The word describes a command, so Balanced says "just" and Readable "fair". Literal keeps "righteous".

records.source: Τὸ οὖν ἀγαθὸν ἐμοὶ ἐγένετο θάνατος;
records.gloss: The then good to me became death?
pieces: Did something good, then, become death to me?

L.13: Did then what [is] good become death to me?

R.13: Then did something good cause my death?

decisions.choice: what is good: the law
decisions.reason: "The good" takes up verse 12, where the commandment is called good. The question is whether the good law was itself the cause of death.

records.source: μὴ γένοιτο· ἀλλὰ ἡ ἁμαρτία, ἵνα φανῇ ἁμαρτία διὰ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ μοι κατεργαζομένη θάνατον· ἵνα γένηται καθ’ ὑπερβολὴν ἁμαρτωλὸς ἡ ἁμαρτία διὰ τῆς ἐντολῆς.
records.gloss: May it not be; but the sin, so that it might appear sin, through the good to me producing death, so that might become beyond measure sinful the sin through the commandment.
pieces: Certainly not! Sin was the cause. It used what was good to work death in me, so that sin would be seen for what it really is. Through the commandment sin showed itself sinful past all measure.

L.13: May it not be! Rather, [it was] sin, so that it might be shown [to be] sin, working death in me through what [is] good, so that through the commandment sin might become sinful beyond measure.

R.13: Of course not! Sin did it. Sin used something good to kill me. This showed what sin really is. The command made it clear how terribly evil sin is.

decisions.choice: it was sin: the verb is supplied from the question
decisions.reason: Paul leaves the verb unsaid: "but sin [became death to me]". The sentence is compressed, but its point is plain: sin, not the law, brought death.

decisions.choice: so that: the purpose served by what happened
decisions.reason: The two "so that" clauses say what came of sin's use of the law: sin was exposed. Many see God's purpose here, as in 5:20, where the law came in so that trespass might increase.

decisions.choice: become sinful beyond measure: be shown as utterly sinful
decisions.reason: Sin's using a good and holy command to kill shows how evil it is. "Beyond measure" is a strong phrase Paul also uses in 2 Corinthians 1:8 and 4:17.

decisions.choice: Sin was the cause (B); Sin did it (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable supply the missing verb (m1). Literal brackets it.

records.source: Οἴδαμεν γὰρ ὅτι ὁ νόμος πνευματικός ἐστιν· ἐγὼ δὲ σάρκινός εἰμι, πεπραμένος ὑπὸ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν.
records.gloss: We know for that the law spiritual is; I but fleshly am, having been sold under the sin.
pieces: We know that the law is spiritual. I, however, am made of flesh, and I have been sold to sin as its slave.

L.14: For we know that the law is spiritual; but I am fleshly, sold under sin.

R.14: We know that the law comes from God's Spirit. But I am a weak human being. I belong to sin, like a slave who has been sold.

decisions.choice: the present tense from 7:14 to 7:25: a debated question the text leaves open
alternatives: a believer's continuing struggle with sin
a person under the law without the Spirit
decisions.reason: From this verse the "I" speaks in the present tense. Some read verses 14-25 as the ongoing struggle of a believer, who loves God's law (verse 22) yet still fails, and note that the summary in verse 25 follows the thanksgiving. Others read them as life under the law without the Spirit, seen with the eyes of faith: the "I" is "sold under sin", while believers have been set free from sin (6:17-18, 8:2), and the Spirit, named often in chapter 8, is not mentioned here. The present tense is kept at every level and no level decides between the readings.

decisions.choice: spiritual: from God's Spirit and belonging to him
decisions.reason: pneumatikos describes what comes from the Spirit of God. The law is God's own, given by his Spirit.

decisions.choice: fleshly: made of flesh, weak and under sin's power
decisions.reason: sarkinos means made of flesh. It describes human beings in their weakness, open to sin's rule (compare 1 Corinthians 3:1, where Paul uses the word of believers who behave as if they were not spiritual).

decisions.choice: sold under sin: sold as a slave to sin
decisions.reason: The picture is of the slave market. Being "sold under" someone is being handed over into his power. Sin is the master (6:16-20).

decisions.choice: sold to sin as its slave (B); like a slave who has been sold (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the picture is (m4). Literal keeps "sold under sin".

decisions.choice: comes from God's Spirit ... a weak human being
decisions.reason: Readable explains "spiritual" (m2) and "fleshly" (m3).

decisions.choice: slave
alternatives: servant
decisions.reason: "Slave" in Balanced and Readable, as the style guide keeps it where slavery itself is the point: sold to sin as a slave is sold at market (m4), the slavery to sin of 6:16-20.

records.heading: Wanting the good, not doing it

records.source: ὃ γὰρ κατεργάζομαι οὐ γινώσκω· οὐ γὰρ ὃ θέλω τοῦτο πράσσω, ἀλλ’ ὃ μισῶ τοῦτο ποιῶ.
records.gloss: What for I produce not I know; not for what I want this I practice, but what I hate this I do.
pieces: What I am doing makes no sense to me. The things I want to do, I fail to do; the things I hate are what I end up doing.

L.15: For what I do, I do not understand; for what I want, this I do not practice, but what I hate, this I do.

R.15: I do not understand myself. I want to do one thing, but I do not do it. I hate something else, but I do it anyway.

decisions.choice: understand: grasp what is happening
alternatives: approve
decisions.reason: ginōskō here is to understand. The speaker cannot make sense of his own actions. Some take it as "approve": I do not approve of what I do. The next clause fits either sense.

decisions.choice: want ... hate: what the will chooses and rejects
decisions.reason: thelō is to want or will. The conflict is between what the speaker wants and what he actually does.

decisions.choice: do: three verbs with the same sense
decisions.reason: Paul varies his words for doing (katergazomai, prassō, poieō). They are used interchangeably through verses 15-20.

decisions.choice: The things I want to do, I fail to do; the things I hate are what I end up doing
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps Paul's balanced pair of clauses but in its own order and words.

records.source: εἰ δὲ ὃ οὐ θέλω τοῦτο ποιῶ, σύμφημι τῷ νόμῳ ὅτι καλός.
records.gloss: If but what not I want this I do, I agree with the law that [it is] good.
pieces: But if I do things I do not want to do, that shows I side with the law: I agree that it is good.

L.16: But if what I do not want, this I do, I agree with the law that [it is] good.

R.16: If I do things I do not want to do, then I am really agreeing that the law is good.

decisions.choice: agree with: concur, say the same thing
decisions.reason: symphēmi is to speak together with someone, to agree. Not wanting the wrong he does shows that the speaker sides with the law's verdict.

decisions.choice: good: right, fine
decisions.reason: kalos varies with agathos (verses 12-13, 18-19) with no difference in meaning.

decisions.choice: that shows I side with the law
decisions.reason: Balanced makes plain how the condition leads to the conclusion.

records.source: νυνὶ δὲ οὐκέτι ἐγὼ κατεργάζομαι αὐτὸ ἀλλὰ ἡ οἰκοῦσα ἐν ἐμοὶ ἁμαρτία.
records.gloss: Now but no longer I produce it but the dwelling in me sin.
pieces: In that case, I am no longer the one doing it; sin is, the sin that has made its home in me.

L.17: But now no longer [is it] I [who] do it, but the sin dwelling in me.

R.17: So I am not the one doing these things. Sin is doing them. It lives inside me.

decisions.choice: now: as things are, in that case
decisions.reason: nyni here draws a logical conclusion, not a point in time.

decisions.choice: not an excuse: the willing self is distinct from the sin that dwells in it
decisions.reason: Paul does not deny responsibility. He separates the self that wants the good from sin, which acts through him like a hostile tenant. The point is that the law is not to blame.

decisions.choice: dwelling: living in, at home in
decisions.reason: oikeō is to live in a house. In 8:9-11 Paul uses the same verb of the Spirit, who lives in believers.

decisions.choice: the sin that has made its home in me
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the picture of a resident in a house (m3).

records.source: οἶδα γὰρ ὅτι οὐκ οἰκεῖ ἐν ἐμοί, τοῦτ’ ἔστιν ἐν τῇ σαρκί μου, ἀγαθόν· τὸ γὰρ θέλειν παράκειταί μοι, τὸ δὲ κατεργάζεσθαι τὸ καλὸν οὔ·
records.gloss: I know for that not dwells in me, that is in the flesh of me, good; the for to want is present with me, the but to produce the good not;
pieces: I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, there is nothing good living. Wanting the good is within my reach; doing it is not.

L.18: For I know that there does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh, [anything] good; for the wanting is present with me, but the doing of the good is not;

R.18: I know that nothing good lives in my sinful self. I want to do what is good, but I am not able to do it.

decisions.choice: that is, in my flesh: a limit on "in me"
decisions.reason: The speaker does not say that nothing good is in him at all, since he wants the good. He means in the flesh, the part of him that sin rules.

decisions.choice: flesh: human nature under sin's sway
decisions.reason: Here "flesh" is the self as weak and ruled by sin, not the body as such (as in verse 5).

decisions.choice: is present: lies at hand, within reach
decisions.reason: parakeimai is to lie ready beside someone. The will to do good is there; the power to do it is not.

decisions.choice: the sentence ends with "not"
alternatives: "I do not find" added at the end
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT ends with a short "not". Later manuscripts add "I do not find", which gives the familiar wording "how to perform what is good I do not find". The shorter text is in the earliest manuscripts. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: my sinful self
alternatives: my flesh
decisions.reason: Readable says what "flesh" means here (m2), as in 7:5. Literal and Balanced keep "flesh".

records.source: οὐ γὰρ ὃ θέλω ποιῶ ἀγαθόν, ἀλλὰ ὃ οὐ θέλω κακὸν τοῦτο πράσσω.
records.gloss: Not for what I want do I good, but what not I want evil this I practice.
pieces: I fail to do the good I want, and the evil I do not want is what I carry out.

L.19: For the good that I want, I do not do, but the evil that I do not want, this I practice.

R.19: I want to do good things, but I do not do them. I do not want to do wrong things, but I do them.

decisions.choice: present tense: what keeps happening
decisions.reason: The verbs describe a repeated pattern, not a single failure.

decisions.choice: good ... evil: right and wrong actions
decisions.reason: Verse 15 is restated with "good" and "evil" in place of "want" and "hate".

records.source: εἰ δὲ ὃ οὐ θέλω τοῦτο ποιῶ, οὐκέτι ἐγὼ κατεργάζομαι αὐτὸ ἀλλὰ ἡ οἰκοῦσα ἐν ἐμοὶ ἁμαρτία.
records.gloss: If but what not I want this I do, no longer I produce it but the dwelling in me sin.
pieces: But if I do what I do not want, then I am no longer the one doing it; sin is, the sin that has made its home in me.

L.20: But if what I do not want, this I do, [it is] no longer I [who] do it, but the sin dwelling in me.

R.20: If I do what I do not want to do, then I am not the one doing it. Sin is doing it. It lives inside me.

decisions.choice: a conclusion that repeats verses 16-17
decisions.reason: Paul repeats verse 16's condition and verse 17's conclusion almost word for word, to drive the point home: the law is good, and the trouble is sin living in the speaker.

records.source: Εὑρίσκω ἄρα τὸν νόμον τῷ θέλοντι ἐμοὶ ποιεῖν τὸ καλὸν ὅτι ἐμοὶ τὸ κακὸν παράκειται·
records.gloss: I find then the law, to the wanting me to do the good, that to me the evil is present;
pieces: This, then, is the law I discover: whenever I set out to do what is good, evil is already there at my side.

L.21: So I find the law that, when I want to do the good, evil is present with me;

R.21: So I find that this law is at work in me: when I want to do what is good, evil is always close beside me.

decisions.choice: the law: a rule or pattern the speaker finds at work
alternatives: the law of Moses
decisions.reason: Here "law" seems to be used in a wider sense: a regular pattern, a principle that always holds. Paul plays on the word through verses 21-25 (the law of God, another law, the law of sin). Some read it as the law of Moses: "I find, as I want to do good by the law, that evil is present". The repetition of "me" makes the Greek awkward either way.

decisions.choice: is present: lies close at hand
decisions.reason: The same verb as in verse 18, now of evil: it is always within reach.

decisions.choice: whenever I set out ... already there at my side (B); always close beside me (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say that the pattern holds every time, which is what a "law" in this sense is (m1).

records.source: συνήδομαι γὰρ τῷ νόμῳ τοῦ θεοῦ κατὰ τὸν ἔσω ἄνθρωπον, βλέπω δὲ ἕτερον νόμον ἐν τοῖς μέλεσίν μου ἀντιστρατευόμενον τῷ νόμῳ τοῦ νοός μου καὶ αἰχμαλωτίζοντά με ἐν τῷ νόμῳ τῆς ἁμαρτίας τῷ ὄντι ἐν τοῖς μέλεσίν μου.
records.gloss: I delight with for in the law of the God according to the inner man, \v 23 I see but another law in the members of me warring against the law of the mind of me and taking captive me in the law of the sin, the [one] being in the members of me.
pieces: In my inner self I gladly agree with God's law.
But I see another law in the parts of my body. It is at war with the law of my mind, and it takes me prisoner to the law of sin that is in those parts of my body.

L.22: For I delight in the law of God according to the inner person,
L.23: but I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and taking me prisoner by the law of sin, which is in my members.

R.22: Deep inside, I love God's law.
R.23: But I see another power at work in my body. It fights against what my mind knows is right. It makes me a prisoner of sin, which is at work in my body.

decisions.choice: the inner person: the self that thinks and wills
alternatives: the new self created by the Spirit
decisions.reason: The inner person is the mind and will, as opposed to the outward life of the body (2 Corinthians 4:16). Some see here the new self that God creates (Ephesians 3:16), which would make the speaker a believer; the phrase itself does not settle that question (see 7:14).

decisions.choice: delight in: rejoice in, gladly agree with
decisions.reason: synēdomai is to take pleasure in something along with others. The speaker's inner self is glad of God's law.

decisions.choice: another law, the law of sin: a ruling power
decisions.reason: "Law" is stretched to mean a power that rules and commands. The "law of sin" is sin's rule, which works through the body and is set against God's law. Paul plays on the word, as in verse 21 and 8:2.

decisions.choice: the law of my mind: God's law as the mind acknowledges it
alternatives: a principle of reason in the mind
decisions.reason: The law of the mind is most likely God's law (verse 22), which the mind approves and serves (verse 25). Some take it as the mind's own rule, a principle of reason.

decisions.choice: warring ... taking prisoner: a military picture
decisions.reason: The other law fights a campaign against the mind and carries the speaker off as a prisoner of war.

decisions.choice: by the law of sin: sin's law holds the prisoner
decisions.reason: The preposition can mean "to" or "by": the speaker is made captive to the law of sin, or by means of it. Either way, sin's rule holds him.

decisions.choice: inner person (L); inner self (B); Deep inside (R)
decisions.reason: The inner person is the speaker himself, so no gender setting is used. "Person" is the human word, which fits a speaker who may stand for others.

decisions.choice: another power ... what my mind knows is right ... a prisoner of sin
decisions.reason: Readable explains each use of "law" by what it means (m3, m4).

records.source: ταλαίπωρος ἐγὼ ἄνθρωπος· τίς με ῥύσεται ἐκ τοῦ σώματος τοῦ θανάτου τούτου;
records.gloss: Wretched I man; who me will rescue out of the body of the death this?
pieces: Wretched man that I am! Who will set me free from this body of death?

L.24: Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me out of the body of this death?

R.24: How miserable I am! Who will set me free from this body that death holds in its grip?

decisions.choice: wretched: miserable, worn down by distress
decisions.reason: talaipōros describes someone in great misery (compare Revelation 3:17). It is a cry of despair, not a confession of a single sin.

decisions.choice: this: the body ruled by death that has just been described
alternatives: this death, the death described in verses 9-13
decisions.reason: "This" may go with "death" (the death of verses 9-13) or with the whole phrase ("this body of death"). The sense comes to the same: the body, through which sin's law works (verse 23), is bound over to death.

decisions.choice: body of death: bodily life under the power of sin and death
decisions.reason: The phrase recalls "the body of sin" in 6:6. Rescue comes in 8:10-11 and 8:23, where God gives life to mortal bodies and redeems them.

decisions.choice: Who will rescue me?: a cry for a rescuer
decisions.reason: The future tense looks for someone to come to the rescue. The answer follows in verse 25 and in chapter 8.

decisions.choice: man, with no gender setting
decisions.reason: anthrōpos here is the speaker himself, so the word is not given the inclusive setting used where people in general are meant.

decisions.choice: the body of this death (L); this body of death (B)
decisions.reason: Literal follows the Greek order and Balanced the more natural one; both carry the sense in m2.

records.source: χάρις τῷ θεῷ διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν.
records.gloss: Thanks to the God through Jesus Christ the Lord of us.
pieces: Thanks be to God through Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} our Lord!

L.25: Thanks [be] to God through Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} our Lord!

R.25: I thank God, who rescues me through Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} our Lord!

decisions.choice: thanks: gratitude given to God
alternatives: grace, God's favor
decisions.reason: charis with "to God" and no verb is the set phrase for giving thanks, as in 6:17 and 2 Corinthians 8:16 and 9:15.

decisions.choice: Thanks be to God
alternatives: I thank God
the grace of God [will rescue me]
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT reads "thanks to God". Some manuscripts read "I thank God", and others "the grace of God" (as if answering the question: the grace of God will rescue me). The meaning is much the same. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: through Jesus Christ: the answer to verse 24
decisions.reason: The thanksgiving answers the cry of verse 24 in short: God rescues through Jesus Christ. Chapter 8 spells this out.

decisions.choice: Thanks (L, B); I thank (R)
alternatives: grace
decisions.reason: The key term is rendered "thanks" here because the sense is gratitude (m1), as in 2 Corinthians 8:16 and 9:15.

decisions.choice: who rescues me
decisions.reason: Readable says what the thanks are for, picking up "rescue" from verse 24 (m3).

records.source: Ἄρα οὖν αὐτὸς ἐγὼ τῷ μὲν νοῒ δουλεύω νόμῳ θεοῦ, τῇ δὲ σαρκὶ νόμῳ ἁμαρτίας.
records.gloss: So then I myself with the indeed mind serve law of God, with the but flesh law of sin.
pieces: So then, I myself serve God's law with my mind, but the law of sin with my flesh.

L.25: So then I myself with the mind serve [the] law of God, but with the flesh [the] law of sin.

R.25: So this is where I am. With my mind I serve God's law. But my sinful self serves the law of sin.

decisions.choice: I myself: the same person in both halves
alternatives: I left to myself, apart from Christ
decisions.reason: autos egō is emphatic: one and the same "I" serves both laws. Some take it as "I left to myself", that is, apart from Christ's help, which would make the sentence a summary of verses 14-24 before chapter 8 brings the answer; others see the believer's ongoing state, after the thanksgiving (see 7:14).

decisions.choice: serve: serve as a slave
decisions.reason: douleuō is the verb of slavery, as in verse 6. The speaker is a slave to two masters at once.

decisions.choice: mind ... flesh: the willing self and the self ruled by sin
decisions.reason: The mind is the inner person of verse 22, which agrees with God's law. The flesh is the self under sin's power (verses 14, 18).

decisions.choice: my sinful self
alternatives: my flesh
decisions.reason: Readable says what "flesh" means here (m3), as in 7:5 and 7:18.

decisions.choice: serves the law of sin
decisions.reason: The Greek leaves the verb to be understood in the second half. Readable repeats it; Literal and Balanced leave it understood.
